opus-5.5.text:
I think it's still very early, but there's real momentum, and honestly it's coming from the ground up, from artists themselves and from the people who love their work. What we've seen over the last couple of years is that a lot of consumers actually care. When people find out that a book cover, an illustration, or a piece of music was generated, there's often a real sense of disappointment, even betrayal. So there's a growing demand for some kind of signal that says a human being made this, a person put their time, skill, and intent into it.

The hard part is verification. Detecting AI-generated content after the fact is a losing game in the long run. Classifiers get better, generators get better, and it becomes an arms race where false positives can really hurt human artists who get wrongly accused. So I think the more durable path is attestation and provenance rather than detection: documenting process, showing work-in-progress, sketches, layered files, time-lapse recordings, and having communities and platforms that vouch for that. Some of that is technical, things like content credentials, and some of it is social, reputation within a community, galleries and publishers who are willing to stand behind a label.

I'd also say certification on its own isn't enough. It helps consumers make informed choices, but it doesn't address the underlying problem, which is that artists' work is being taken without consent to train the very models that compete with them. That's part of why we built tools like Glaze and Nightshade, to give artists some agency back. A "human-made" label and protective tools are complementary. One helps the market value human creativity, the other helps protect it from being exploited in the first place.

So where I see it going: more platforms and publishers adopting human-made policies, more standardization around provenance, and hopefully regulation that backs up consent and transparency. None of it will be perfect, but the fact that people are asking for it at all tells you that human creativity still matters deeply to people, and that's really encouraging.

r001.rationale: The response describes consumers feeling disappointment or betrayal when they learn art was AI-generated, but it does not describe a rapid shift from amazement at AI art’s realism to viewing it as artificial or soulless.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's really the flip side of what we've been doing with Glaze and Nightshade. Those tools are about protection, about giving artists a way to say no. But the other half of the problem is on the demand side: how do people who actually want human-made work find it and trust that it's real?

What I've seen over the last couple of years is that this is emerging bottom-up rather than top-down. It's not coming from the big platforms, because frankly the platforms have very little incentive to make this distinction. It's coming from artists themselves, from communities like Cara, from galleries and small marketplaces that have decided their brand is "no AI here." And it's coming from buyers. There's a real segment of people, commissioners, collectors, publishers, who care about the provenance of what they're paying for, in the same way people care about handmade furniture or organic food. The value isn't just in the pixels, it's in the fact that a person made it.

Now, the hard part is the word "certified." Certification implies verification, and verification is technically very difficult. You cannot reliably detect AI-generated images after the fact. The detectors don't work well, and they get worse every month as the models improve. So anything built on "we'll scan your image and tell you if it's human" is going to fail. What's more promising is provenance that gets attached at creation time, things like C2PA-style content credentials, process documentation, layered source files, timelapse recordings. The idea is you prove you made it by showing the making, not by having someone inspect the result.

But I'd be careful about overselling that too. Those systems can be gamed, metadata can be stripped, and the burden falls on the artist, who is already the party with the least time and resources. And there's a real risk that if "human-certified" becomes a premium label, it becomes something only established artists can afford to maintain, while the students and emerging artists who are most vulnerable get left out.

So where do I think it goes? I think in the near term it looks less like a single global certification and more like a web of trust. Communities, platforms, and individual reputations that people learn to rely on. Over time, if there's enough economic pressure from buyers and ideally some regulatory pressure around disclosure, those standards can consolidate. But the thing I'd stress is that the movement can't just be technical. It has to be cultural. People have to actually value the human part of the work. The technology can support that, but it can't create it.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses buyers valuing human-made work and the difficulty of verifying it, but does not describe public reactions shifting from amazement at AI art’s realism to seeing it as artificial or soulless.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re going to see more demand for knowing where art comes from and what role a person played in creating it. For some people, the finished image is what matters. For others, the artist’s story, their intent, and the work that went into it are a big part of the value. Certification could help that second group make choices that reflect what they care about.

The hard part is deciding what you’re certifying. Does “human-created” mean no generative AI anywhere in the process? How do you establish that without asking artists to document every brushstroke? If the process becomes expensive or intrusive, it could end up excluding the very people it’s supposed to support.

So I’d expect this to develop through communities first—artists, buyers, and galleries agreeing on standards they trust. A label can help, but the trust behind that label is what will make it meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses demand for provenance and trust in certification, but does not describe a rapid shift from amazement at AI art’s realism to seeing it as artificial or soulless.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s going to be growing interest in knowing that something was created by a person. Part of what people value in art is the connection to the artist—their experience, their intent, and the story behind the work. A certification could help preserve that connection, especially as it becomes harder to tell how something was made just by looking at it.

The challenge is making that certification meaningful. Who verifies it? What does “human-created” mean when artists use digital tools, some of which have AI built in? And can you make the process accessible to independent artists? I could see this developing through communities and trusted relationships first. Whether it becomes a broader movement will depend on whether audiences care enough about that distinction to support the artists making it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses growing interest in identifying human-created art, but does not describe a rapid shift in public reactions from amazement at AI art’s realism to viewing it as artificial or soulless.
